9.1Back to the Alkanes: Formulas, Carbons and Names
✔ Objectives of this chapter • Recognize the functional groups –OH, C=O, –COOH and –COO– and the families they define. • Write the general formulas of saturated noncyclic open-chain alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters. • Name these compounds (IUPAC) and write their condensed and skeletal formulas from their names. • Classify an alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary. • Find the isomers of a formula (functional, positional and skeletal). • Use the general formula and the molar mass to find a molecular formula.★ Scope of the chapter Only open-chain, saturated noncyclic, monofunctional compounds are studied: saturated noncyclic monoalcohols, aldehydes, ketones, saturated noncyclic monocarboxylic acids and esters. The other groups (ethers, acid halides, acid anhydrides, amides, amines) and the aromatic compounds are not part of this booklet.

9.1.1 Five ways to write the same molecule

★ Reading a skeletal formula
• Each end of a line and each corner is a carbon atom.
• The hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not written; each carbon has four bonds, so the missing bonds are C–H bonds.
• Atoms other than C and H (here O) are written, with the hydrogen atoms attached to them (–OH).

9.1.2 Types of carbon atoms

CarbonBonded toExample in CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3
Primary (1°)1 other carbonthe three CH3 groups
Secondary (2°)2 other carbonsthe CH2 group
Tertiary (3°)3 other carbonsthe CH group
Neo (quaternary)4 other carbonsno hydrogen atom (e.g. the central C of neopentane)
◆ Alkyl radicals R–
An alkyl radical is an alkane that has lost one hydrogen atom: CnH2n+2 → CnH2n+1– (R–). Names: CH3– methyl, CH3CH2– ethyl, CH3CH2CH2– 1-propyl, (CH3)2CH– 2-propyl. There are four butyl radicals: 1-butyl, 2-butyl, 2-methylpropyl and 2-methyl-2-propyl (the old “tertiary butyl”).

9.1.4 Rules of IUPAC naming (reminder)

★ The four rules
1. Choose the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms (with the greatest number of branches): it gives the parent’s name.
2. Number it in the direction that gives the lowest numbers (locants) to the branches: compare the sets of numbers one by one (2, 5 is lower than 3, 6).
3. Name every branch (methyl, ethyl …) with its locant; use di, tri … for identical branches.
4. List the branches in alphabetical order, ignoring di, tri: ethyl before methyl. Name = locants-branches + parent.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 What does each corner of a skeletal formula represent?
A carbon atom.
2 How many carbon neighbors has a secondary carbon?
Two.
3 General formula of an alkyl radical?
CnH2n+1–.
4 How many butyl radicals exist?
Four.
5 Which comes first in a name: ethyl or methyl?
Ethyl (alphabetical order).
6 Name of CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3?
2-methylbutane.

9.1.5 Exercise: Practice: carbons and names

9.1.6 Exercise: Level 1 – Types of carbon

For 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, (CH3)3CCH2CH(CH3)2:
a) draw the skeletal formula;
b) count the primary, secondary, tertiary and neo carbons.
✔ Solution
a) A chain of five carbons (zigzag) with two methyl groups on carbon 2 and one methyl group on carbon 4.
b) Primary: 5 (the five CH3); secondary: 1 (the CH2); tertiary: 1 (the CH); neo: 1 (the C bonded to four carbons). Total 8 carbons ✔.

9.1.7 Exercise: Level 2 – Name the alkanes

Give the IUPAC name.
a) CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH3
b) CH3CH2CH(CH2CH3)CH2CH3
c) CH3C(CH3)2CH2CH3
d) CH3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3
✔ Solution
a) 2-methylpentane.
b) the longest chain has five carbons (the ethyl branch is on the middle one): 3-ethylpentane.
c) 2,2-dimethylbutane.
d) 2,3-dimethylpentane.
9.2Functional Groups and Families
◆ Functional group
A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms that is responsible for the chemical properties (the reactivity) of a molecule and defines its family (class). Compounds that have the same functional group and the same general formula form a homologous series: they differ by one or more CH2 groups.
FamilyFunctional groupGeneral formulaWritten asEnding in the name
Alcoholshydroxyl –OHCnH2n+1OH or CnH2n+2OR–OHalkanol
Aldehydescarbonyl at the end of the chain –CHOCnH2nOR–CHOalkanal
Ketonescarbonyl inside the chain >C=OCnH2nOR–CO–R′alkanone
Carboxylic acidscarboxyl –COOHCnH2n+1COOH or CnH2nO2R–COOHalkanoic acid
Estersester group –COO–CnH2nO2R–COO–R′alkyl alkanoate
✎ Values of n Alcohols: n ≥ 1 (methanol). Aldehydes: n ≥ 1 (methanal). Ketones: n ≥ 3 (propanone). Carboxylic acids: n ≥ 1 (methanoic acid, n counts the carbon of the carboxyl group). Esters: n ≥ 2 (methyl methanoate). In these formulas n is the total number of carbon atoms (except in CnH2n+1COOH, where n is the number of carbons of R).★ Functional isomers in the same formula Aldehydes and ketones have the same general formula CnH2nO; carboxylic acids and esters have the same general formula CnH2nO2. Compounds of these pairs are functional isomers (section 9.7).
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 What is a functional group?
The atom or group of atoms responsible for the properties and the family of the compound.
2 Functional group of alcohols?
Hydroxyl –OH.
3 Functional group of carboxylic acids?
Carboxyl –COOH.
4 General formula of aldehydes and ketones?
CnH2nO.
5 General formula of carboxylic acids and esters?
CnH2nO2.
6 What is the smallest ketone?
Propanone (n = 3).

9.3Alcohols: The Hydroxyl Group
◆ Saturated noncyclic monoalcohols
The hydroxyl group –OH is bonded to a saturated noncyclic carbon. A saturated noncyclic monoalcohol has one –OH group and the general formula:
The alcohols are named with the suffix –ol: alkanol. The carbon that bears the –OH group is the carbinol carbon: carbon the classify the monoalcohol (primary, secondary or teritairy).
nCondensed formulaNameCommon name
1CH3OHmethanolwood alcohol (toxic)
2CH3CH2OH or C2H5OHethanolethyl alcohol, spirit
3CH3CH2CH2OH1-propanol
3CH3CH(OH)CH32-propanolisopropyl alcohol
4CH3CH2CH2CH2OH1-butanol
5CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH1-pentanol

9.3.1 Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols

★ Classes of alcohols
Primary (1°): the carbinol carbon is bonded to one carbon (or to none, in methanol): R–CH2–OH.
Secondary (2°): the carbinol carbon is bonded to two carbons: R–CH(OH)–R′.
Tertiary (3°): the carbinol carbon is bonded to three carbons: R–C(OH)(R′)–R″.

The class is that of the carbon bearing the –OH, not of the alcohol as a whole.

9.3.2 IUPAC naming of alcohols

★ Rules
1. The parent chain is the longest chain that contains the carbinol carbon (it is not always the longest chain of the molecule).
2. Number the chain so that the –OH group gets the lowest number; this rule has priority over the position of the branches.
3. Name: locants-branches (alphabetical) + parent name with the ending “–ol” preceded by the locant of OH. The final “e” of the alkane is dropped: butane → butanol.
✔ Correction to remember • In an alcohol, –OH is expressed as the suffix –ol, not as the prefix “hydroxy”. The prefix hydroxy is used only when another group has priority. • There is no rule “hetero groups before alkyl groups”: all prefixes are placed in alphabetical order. Example: CH3CH2CH(CH2CH3)CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 3-ethyl-5-methyl-4-heptanol (and not “4-hydroxy-3-ethyl-5-methylheptane”); CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH(CH3)CH3 is 5-methyl-3-hexanol (and not “3-hydroxy-5-methylhexane”).✎ Properties in one sentence The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds: an alcohol boils at a much higher temperature than the alkane of similar molar mass, and the first alcohols are soluble in water.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 General formula of a saturated noncyclic monoalcohol?
CnH2n+2O.
2 Suffix of alcohols?
–ol.
3 What is the class of 2-propanol?
Secondary.
4 What is the class of 2-methyl-2-propanol?
Tertiary.
5 Which number does the –OH group get in the numbering?
The lowest possible.
6 Name of CH3CH2CH2OH?
1-propanol.

9.3.3 Exercise: Practice: alcohols

9.3.4 Exercise: Level 1 – Name and classify

Name each alcohol and give its class. a) CH3CH2CH2CH2OH b) CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 c) (CH3)2CHCH2OH d) (CH3)3COH e) CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3 f) CH3CH(CH3)CH(OH)CH3✔ Solution a) 1-butanol: primary. b) 2-butanol: secondary. c) 2-methyl-1-propanol: primary. d) 2-methyl-2-propanol: tertiary. e) 3-pentanol: secondary. f) 3-methyl-2-butanol: secondary (the chain is numbered from the end that gives the –OH the number 2).

9.3.5 Exercise: Level 2 – Write the formulas

Write the condensed formula, the molecular formula and the class of:
a) 2-pentanol
b) 3-methyl-2-pentanol
c) 2,2-dimethyl-1-propanol
d) 2-methyl-2-butanol.
✔ Solution
a) CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3, C5H12O, secondary.
b) CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH2CH3, C6H14O, secondary.

9.3.6 Exercise: Level 3 – Find the mistakes in the names

Each name is wrong. Draw the structure it describes and give the correct name.
a) 3-butanol
b) 2-ethyl-1-propanol
c) 1-methyl-1-propanol
d) 2,3-dimethyl-4-pentanol
e) 4-hydroxy-3-ethyl-5-methylheptane
✔ Solution
a) CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3: numbering from the other end gives the lowest number to OH: 2-butanol.
b) HOCH2CH(CH2CH3)CH3: the longest chain has four carbons: 2-methyl-1-butanol.
c) CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3: the longest chain is butane: 2-butanol.
d) CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH3: –OH must get the lowest number: 3,4-dimethyl-2-pentanol.
e) OH is expressed as “–ol” and the branches are alphabetical: 3-ethyl-5-methyl-4-heptanol.
9.4Carbonyl Compounds: Aldehydes and Ketones
◆ The carbonyl group
The carbonyl group is a carbon atom doubly bonded to an oxygen atom, >C=O. The compounds that contain it have the general formula CnH2nO:
• Aldehydes R–CHO: the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain (the carbon is bonded to one hydrogen atom and one oxygen atom)..
• Ketones R–CO–R′: the carbonyl group is inside the chain, bonded to two carbons.
★ IUPAC naming
• Aldehydes: alkanal. The CHO carbon is always carbon 1, so no locant is written for it: methanal, ethanal, propanal, 2-methylbutanal.
• Ketones: alkanone. The chain is the longest chain that contains the C=O, numbered so that the C=O gets the lowest number, written before the ending: 2-butanone, 3-pentanone, 3-methyl-2-butanone. A ketone has at least 3 carbons (propanone). When only one position is possible, the locant can be omitted (propanone, butanone).
AldehydeFormulaCommon nameKetoneFormulaCommon name
methanalHCHOformaldehydepropanoneCH3COCH3acetone
ethanalCH3CHOacetaldehyde2-butanoneCH3COCH2CH3
propanalCH3CH2CHO2-pentanoneCH3COCH2CH2CH3
butanalCH3CH2CH2CHO3-pentanoneCH3CH2COCH2CH3
✔ Correction to remember
• Aldehyde names have no locant for –CHO: “2-propanal” is wrong, the name is propanal.
• A ketone group is never at the end of the chain: “1-butanone” does not exist (it would be butanal).
• Do not confuse the carbonyl group >C=O (aldehydes and ketones) with the carboxyl group –COOH (acids).
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 General formula of aldehydes and ketones?
CnH2nO.
2 Where is the carbonyl group in an aldehyde?
At the end of the chain (carbon 1).
3 Ending of a ketone name?
–one.
4 Smallest ketone?
Propanone.
5 Name of CH3CH2CH2CHO?
Butanal.
6 Name of CH3COCH2CH3?
2-butanone (butanone).

9.4.4 Exercise: Level 3 – Find the mistakes

Correct each statement.
a) “2-propanal is an aldehyde.”
b) “1-butanone is a ketone.”
c) “2-methyl-3-butanone is a ketone.”
) “Ethanone is the simplest ketone.”
e) “Aldehydes have the general formula CnH2n+2O.”
✔ Solution
a) The CHO carbon is carbon 1: the name is propanal.
b) A ketone C=O cannot be at the end: CH3CH2CH2CHO is butanal; the ketone is 2-butanone.
c) The C=O must get the lowest number: 3-methyl-2-butanone.
d) A ketone needs two carbons around the C=O: the simplest is propanone.
e) CnH2nO (CnH2n+2O is the formula of the alcohols).
9.5Carboxylic Acids: The Carboxyl Group
◆ Saturated noncyclic monocarboxylic acids The carboxyl group –COOH (a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on the same carbon) is at the end of the chain. The general formula is: Here the formula CnH2n+1COOH counts n carbons in R, and CnH2nO2 counts all the carbons: for ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, it is C2H4O2.★ IUPAC naming: alkanoic acid The carboxyl carbon is always carbon 1, so no locant is written for the group. The ending of the alkane “–e” is replaced by “–oic acid”. Branches are numbered from the carboxyl carbon and named in alphabetical order: 2-methylpropanoic acid, 3-methylbutanoic acid.
NameFormulaCommon name
methanoic acidHCOOHformic acid (ants)
ethanoic acidCH3COOHacetic acid (vinegar)
propanoic acidCH3CH2COOHpropionic acid
butanoic acidCH3CH2CH2COOHbutyric acid (rancid butter)
pentanoic acidCH3(CH2)3COOHvaleric acid
✎ Reaction with a base (used in titrations) A carboxylic acid is neutralized by a strong base such as sodium hydroxide. One mole of a monoacid reacts with one mole of NaOH: CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2O (sodium ethanoate). The amount of acid is found from the volume of base needed: n(NaOH) = n(RCOOH) at the equivalence.✔ Correction to remember Benzoic acid, C6H5COOH, is an aromatic acid: it does not follow the general formula CnH2nO2 and is not studied here.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 General formula of saturated noncyclic monocarboxylic acids?
CnH2nO2.
2 Where is the carboxyl group?
At the end of the chain (carbon 1).
3 Ending in the name?
–oic acid.
4 Name of CH3CH2COOH?
Propanoic acid.
5 How many NaOH per COOH in a titration?
One.
6 Name of (CH3)2CHCOOH?
2-methylpropanoic acid.

9.5.4 Exercise: Level 3 – Titration of an acid

115 mg of a saturated noncyclic monocarboxylic acid is dissolved in 10 mL of water and titrated with a sodium hydroxide solution of mass concentration 10 g/L, in the presence of phenolphthalein; the persistent pink color appears when 10 mL of the base have been added (M(NaOH) = 40 g/mol).
a) Write the equation of the reaction.
b) Calculate the molar concentration of the base.
c) Calculate the molar mass of the acid.
d) Deduce its formula and its name.
✔ Solution
a) RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H2O.
b) C = 10/40 = 0.25 mol/L.
c) n(NaOH) = 0.25 × 0.010 = 2.5×10−3 mol = n(acid); M = 0.115 / 2.5×10−3 = 46 g/mol.
The acid is HCOOH, methanoic acid.
9.6Esters: The Ester Group
◆ Esters
The ester group –COO– is formed when the –OH of a carboxylic acid is replaced by an –OR′ group. Saturated noncyclic esters have the general formula CnH2nO2 (R–COO–R′), the same as the acids. They are obtained from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (esterification, Chapter of chemical equilibrium):
★ IUPAC naming: alkyl alkanoate
An ester has two parts, named as two words:
• the alkanoate part comes from the acid (the carbon chain with the C=O, numbered from the carbonyl carbon): ethanoate, propanoate …
• the alkyl part comes from the alcohol and is bonded to the oxygen with two single bonds: methyl, ethyl, 1-methylethyl …
Name = alkyl + alkanoate (the alkyl is written first, but the acid part is written first in the formula R–COO–R′).
⚠ Two methods
From the formula to the name: find the –COO– group, count the carbons on the carbonyl side (alkanoate) and on the oxygen side (alkyl). CH3CH2COOCH3: three carbons with the C=O → propanoate; one carbon on the O → methyl: methyl propanoate.
From the name to the formula: write the acid part R–COO–, then the alkyl group: ethyl butanoate = CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3.
✔ Correction to remember
Write the name of an ester as two words: “methyl ethanoate” (not “methylethanoate”). The first word names the alcohol part.
✎ Everyday life
Esters are responsible for the smell of fruits and flowers (for example ethyl butanoate: pineapple) and are used as solvents and in perfumes. Their hydrolysis (with water) is the inverse of the esterification.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 Functional group of esters?
–COO–.
2 General formula of saturated noncyclic esters?
CnH2nO2.
3 Which part of the name comes from the alcohol?
The first word (the alkyl).
4 Name of CH3COOCH2CH3?
Ethyl ethanoate.
5 Smallest ester?
Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH3.
6 Do acids and esters have the same general formula?
Yes, CnH2nO2.

9.6.2 Exercise: Level 1 – Name

Name each ester.
a) CH3COOCH2CH2CH3
b) HCOOCH3
c) CH3CH2COOCH(CH3)2
d) CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3
e) (CH3)2CHCOOCH3
✔ Solution
a) propyl ethanoate.
b) methyl methanoate.
c) 1-methylethyl propanoate (isopropyl propanoate).
d) ethyl butanoate.
e) methyl 2-methylpropanoate.

9.6.3 Exercise: Level 2 – Acid and alcohol of an ester

For each ester give the acid and the alcohol from which it is obtained and write the esterification equation:
a) ethyl butanoate
b) propyl methanoate
c) 1-methylethyl ethanoate
d) methyl 2-methylpropanoate.
✔ Solution
a) butanoic acid + ethanol: CH3CH2CH2COOH + C2H5OH ↔ CH3CH2CH2COOC2H5 + H2O.
b) methanoic acid + 1-propanol: HCOOH + CH3CH2CH2OH ↔ HCOOCH2CH2CH3 + H2O.
c) ethanoic acid + 2-propanol: CH3COOH + CH3CH(OH)CH3 ↔ CH3COOCH(CH3)2 + H2O.
d) 2-methylpropanoic acid + methanol: (CH3)2CHCOOH + CH3OH ↔ (CH3)2CHCOOCH3 + H2O.

9.6.4 Exercise: Level 3 – An ester of molar mass 116 g/mol

A saturated noncyclic ester has a molar mass of 116 g/mol. (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
a) Find its molecular formula.
b) The ester is prepared from ethanoic acid. Write its formula and its name, and the name of the alcohol used.
c) Give the name of another ester of the same formula made from methanoic acid.
✔ Solution
b) The alkyl part has 6 − 2 = 4 carbons: for the unbranched one, CH3COOCH2CH2CH2CH3, butyl ethanoate, from 1-butanol.
c) The alkyl part must have 5 carbons: HCOOCH2CH2CH2CH2CH3, pentyl methanoate.
9.7Isomerism
◆ Isomers Isomers are different compounds that have the same molecular formula (and therefore the same molar mass) but different structural formulas, so different names, physical and chemical properties.★ Types of structural isomerism 1. Functional isomers: same molecular formula, different functional groups. In this chapter: aldehydes and ketones (CnH2nO) and carboxylic acids and esters (CnH2nO2). 2. Positional isomers: same carbon skeleton and same functional group, but the group is in a different position (1-propanol and 2-propanol). 3. Skeletal (chain) isomers: the carbon skeleton is different (1-butanol and 2-methyl-1-propanol).

9.7.1 Isomers of an alcohol: C4H10O

PairRelationshipReason
A and Bpositionalsame skeleton (butane), OH on carbon 1 or 2
C and Dpositionalsame skeleton (2-methylpropane), OH on carbon 1 or 2
A and C | B and Dskeletalthe skeleton changes, the OH stays at the same position
A and D | B and Cskeletal and positionalthe skeleton and the position of OH both change
★ Method to find the isomers
1. Find the family and the general formula from the molecular formula.
2. Draw the carbon skeletons (unbranched chain, then chains with one branch, then two branches …), without repeating a skeleton.
3. Put the functional group at every different position of each skeleton (two positions that are equivalent by symmetry give the same compound).
4. Name every isomer and check that two names do not describe the same compound.

9.7.2 Functional isomers

Molecular formulaFamilyIsomersNumber
C3H8Oalcohols1-propanol, 2-propanol2
C4H10Oalcohols1-butanol, 2-butanol, 2-methyl-1-propanol, 2-methyl-2-propanol4
C5H12Oalcohols3 pentanols, 4 branched C5 alcohols (see exercise)8
C3H6Oaldehydes and ketonespropanal, propanone2
C4H8Oaldehydes and ketonesbutanal, 2-methylpropanal, 2-butanone3
C5H10Oaldehydes and ketones4 aldehydes and 3 ketones7
C3H6O2acids and esterspropanoic acid, methyl ethanoate, ethyl methanoate3
C4H8O2acids and esters2 acids and 4 esters6
C5H10O2acids and esters4 acids and 9 esters13
✔ Correction to remember
A list of functional isomers that includes alkenes and cycloalkanes (CnH2n) or alcohols and ethers (CnH2n+2O) belongs to other families: for the compounds of this chapter, the functional isomers are the pairs aldehyde / ketone and acid / ester.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 What do isomers have in common?
The same molecular formula.
2 Name the three types of structural isomerism.
Functional, positional, skeletal.
3 Functional isomers of an aldehyde?
Ketones (same CnH2nO).
4 Functional isomers of a carboxylic acid?
Esters (same CnH2nO2).
5 How many alcohols have the formula C4H10O?
Four.
6 1-propanol and 2-propanol are … isomers.
Positional.

9.7.3 Exercise: Practice: isomers

9.7.4 Exercise: Level 1 – Type of isomerism

State the type of isomerism between:
a) butanal and 2-butanone
b) 1-pentanol and 2-pentanol
c) butanoic acid and methyl propanoate
d) 1-butanol and 2-methyl-1-propanol
e) 3-pentanone and 2-pentanone.
✔ Solution
a) functional (aldehyde / ketone, C4H8O).
b) positional (same skeleton).
c) functional (acid / ester, C4H8O2).
d) skeletal (same position of OH, different skeleton).
e) positional (same skeleton, C=O on carbon 2 or 3).

9.7.5 Exercise: Level 2 – The pentanols

Write the names and classes of all the alcohols of formula C5H12O.
✔ Solution
The skeleton of pentane: 1-pentanol (1°), 2-pentanol (2°), 3-pentanol (2°).
The skeleton of 2-methylbutane: 2-methyl-1-butanol (1°), 3-methyl-1-butanol (1°), 2-methyl-2-butanol (3°), 3-methyl-2-butanol (2°).
The skeleton of 2,2-dimethylpropane: 2,2-dimethyl-1-propanol (1°).
Total: 8 alcohols.

9.7.6 Exercise: Level 2 – C5H10O: aldehydes and ketones

Write and name all the carbonyl compounds of formula C5H10O.
✔ Solution
Aldehydes: pentanal, 2-methylbutanal, 3-methylbutanal, 2,2-dimethylpropanal (4).
Ketones: 2-pentanone, 3-pentanone, 3-methyl-2-butanone (3).
Total: 7 (the 4 aldehydes are functional isomers of the 3 ketones).

9.7.7 Exercise: Level 3 – C4H8O2

a) Write the structural formula and the name of the esters of formula C4H8O2.
b) Which one is formed from methanoic acid and 2-propanol?
c) Why can the same formula also be an acid?
✔ Solution
a) HCOOCH2CH2CH3 propyl methanoate; HCOOCH(CH3)2 1-methylethyl methanoate; CH3COOCH2CH3 ethyl ethanoate; CH3CH2COOCH3 methyl propanoate.
b) 1-methylethyl methanoate (isopropyl methanoate).
c) Acids and esters have the same general formula CnH2nO2: butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid are also C4H8O2.
9.8Finding the Family and the Formula from Data
★ Molar mass and general formula When the family of the compound is known (or suspected), the molar mass gives n: • Alcohol: M = 14n + 18. • Aldehyde or ketone: M = 14n + 16. • Acid or ester: M = 14n + 32. Example: a saturated noncyclic acid of M = 88 g/mol: 14n + 32 = 88 ⇒ n = 4, C4H8O2.★ Combustion equations Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water: For the carbonyl compounds, the acids and the esters, n(CO2) = n(H2O) (same number of moles of each product): this tells you that the formula is CnH2nOx.
Example 1. The combustion of 0.74 g of a saturated noncyclic monoalcohol gives 1.76 g of carbon dioxide (M(CO2) = 44 g/mol).

0.74n = 0.040(14n + 18) = 0.56n + 0.72 ⇒ 0.18n = 0.72 ⇒ n = 4: C4H10O (M = 74 g/mol; 0.74/74 = 0.010 mol ✔).

★ Elemental analysis (from Chapter 12 of Grade 11)
Empirical formula: divide the percentages by the atomic masses and by the smallest result. Then M = (E.F.)x.
✔ Quick Check – Test Yourself
1 M of an alcohol as a function of n?
14n + 18.
2 M of an aldehyde or ketone?
14n + 16.
3 M of an acid or ester?
14n + 32.
4 Relation between n(CO2) and n(H2O) for CnH2nO2?
Equal.
5 O₂ coefficient for the combustion of CnH2nO2?
(3n − 2)/2.
6 Molar mass of C4H8O2?
88 g/mol.

9.8.1 Exercise: Practice: finding formulas

9.8.2 Exercise: Level 1 – Formula from M

Find the molecular formula of a saturated noncyclic compound of the given family and molar mass.
a) alcohol, M = 60 g/mol
b) acid, M = 74 g/mol
c) aldehyde, M = 58 g/mol
d) ester, M = 102 g/mol.
✔ Solution
a) 14n + 18 = 60 ⇒ n = 3: C3H8O.
b) 14n + 32 = 74 ⇒ n = 3: C3H6O2 (propanoic acid).
c) 14n + 16 = 58 ⇒ n = 3: C3H6O (propanal).
d) 14n + 32 = 102 ⇒ n = 5: C5H10O2.

9.8.3 Exercise: Level 2 – Percentage composition

A compound has the mass percentages C = 40 % and H = 6.7 %, and a molar mass of 30 g/mol (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16). a) Show that it contains oxygen and calculate its percentage.
b) Find its empirical and molecular formulas.
c) It contains a carbonyl group at the end of the chain. Name it and write its structural formula.
✔ Solution
a) 40 + 6.7 = 46.7 < 100: oxygen is present: %O = 100 − 46.7 = 53.3 %.
b) 40/12 = 3.33; 6.7/1 = 6.7; 53.3/16 = 3.33 ⇒ ratio 1 : 2 : 1: E.F. CH2O (M = 30) ⇒ x = 1: CH2O.
c) It is an aldehyde: methanal, HCHO: H–C(=O)–H.

9.8.4 Exercise: Level 2 – The same percentages, M = 60 g/mol

The same percentages (C = 40 %, H = 6.7 %) correspond to a compound of molar mass 60 g/mol.
a) Find its molecular formula.
b) Write all the saturated noncyclic compounds of this formula that are carboxylic acids or esters, and name them.
✔ Solution
a) E.F. CH2O (30): x = 60/30 = 2 ⇒ C2H4O2 (that is CnH2nO2, n = 2).
b) ethanoic acid CH3COOH and methyl methanoate HCOOCH3 (the formula allows no other isomer).

9.9.6 Exercise: Level 2 – Name all the compounds

Name each compound (g to l) and give its family.
✔ Solution
g) 3-pentanone (ketone).
h) 2-methyl-1-butanol (primary alcohol).
i) 2-pentanone (ketone): number from the right so that the C=O gets 2.

9.9.7 Exercise: Level 2 – Find the incorrect formulas

In each group, one formula or name is wrong. Remove it and justify.
a) 2-propanol, 3-butanol, 1-butanol.
b) CH3COOCH3, CH3COCH3, CH3CHCOOH.
c) 2-propanal, 2-butanone, butanal.
✔ Solution
a) 3-butanol is wrong: numbering from the other end gives the lowest number to OH: 2-butanol.
b) CH3CHCOOH has a carbon with only three bonds (it lacks hydrogen atoms): CH3CH2COOH is correct.
c) 2-propanal does not exist: the aldehyde carbon is carbon 1 (propanal).

9.9.8 Exercise: Level 3 – Which family?

The combustion of 1.16 g of a saturated noncyclic compound D (only C, H, O) gives 2.64 g of carbon dioxide and 1.08 g of water. (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, M(CO2) = 44, M(H2O) = 18)
a) Compare n(CO2) and n(H2O). What does it tell you?
b) Find the formula of D.
c) D is an aldehyde: write its possible formulas and names.
✔ Solution
a) n(CO2) = 2.64/44 = 0.060 mol; n(H2O) = 1.08/18 = 0.060 mol: equal, so D is of type CnH2nOx (carbonyl compound, acid or ester).
b) m(C) = 0.72 g; m(H) = 0.12 g; m(O) = 1.16 − 0.84 = 0.32 g ⇒ n(O) = 0.020 mol. C : H : O = 0.060 : 0.12 : 0.020 = 3 : 6 : 1: C3H6O, M = 58 (1.16/58 = 0.020 mol ✔).
c) The only aldehyde is propanal, CH3CH2CHO; its functional isomer is propanone.
